question: Are bird numbers around Elephants by the Lake increasing or falling over the last five years? Use public data if that is all we have, but tell me whether the trend is real enough to guide restoration choices.
answer:
I’m going to identify what `Elephants by the Lake` refers to, then look for the best nearby bird-monitoring dataset and assess whether the last five years show a meaningful trend.I found two overlapping references: `Elephants By The Lake` is a restoration project in the Eastern Ghats, and there is also an `eBird` hotspot with the same name in Krishnagiri. I’m now anchoring the analysis to that hotspot and checking whether the recent bird records suggest a real biological trend or mainly changing observer effort.I have the site identity but not yet the time series. Next I’m probing `eBird` and other open sources for yearly checklist/species counts near the hotspot so I can separate a real bird trend from increased observer effort.The `recent checklists` page does expose individual checklist dates and species totals, so I’m parsing it now to see whether the yearly filter works and what the observation effort looks like by year.The hotspot appears to have public records only from late 2024 onward, so a strict five-year site trend may not exist. I’m checking whether a broader nearby locality in the same valley can extend the time series enough to be decision-useful.I found that the summary page can misstate some checklist species totals, so I’m validating against the individual public checklist pages before drawing any trend line.I’ve launched a full scrape of the public `eBird` checklists for the hotspot so I can compare like-for-like complete checklists rather than raw page summaries. Next step is to inspect those normalized yearly metrics and decide whether any apparent trend is strong enough for restoration decisions.I have enough to answer: the public record at the hotspot is too short and too effort-sensitive for a real five-year trend, and the best normalized signal is mixed rather than steadily up or down. I’m pulling one last bit of landscape context from local surveys so I can say what this does and does not justify for restoration.## Bottom Line
No credible five-year increase or decline can be established yet for birds at `Elephants by the Lake`.

The public record at the actual `eBird` hotspot for `Elephants by the Lake` only runs from **10 Oct 2024 to 22 Jun 2026**, not five full years, and the checklist mix changes a lot across time. The raw public data show an apparent dip in 2025, but that signal is **not stable enough** to treat as a real biological decline or increase for restoration planning. The safest reading is: **bird use of the site looks variable, not clearly trending up or down**. [eBird hotspot](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021), [recent checklists](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021/recent-checklists), [sample checklist with map link](https://ebird.org/checklist/S304431787)

## What The Public Data Say
I anchored the analysis to the `eBird` hotspot associated with the restoration site in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu. `EBTL` itself describes the project as a 70-acre restoration site in the foothills of degraded Eastern Ghats forest near Krishnagiri. [EBTL site](https://ebtl.earth/)

From the public hotspot record, I extracted **168 checklist links** and successfully validated **161 public checklist pages** at the same hotspot name and coordinate (`12.7338913,78.1833887`) from the map links on the checklist pages. [recent checklists](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021/recent-checklists), [28 Feb 2026 checklist](https://ebird.org/checklist/S304431787), [23 Feb 2026 checklist](https://ebird.org/checklist/S303183063)

Using those validated checklists, the raw yearly pattern looks like this:

| Year | Date coverage | Checklists used | Mean species/checklist | Mean individuals/checklist* | Median duration |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2024 | Oct-Dec only | 34 | 23.3 | 53.2 | 53 min |
| 2025 | full year | 105 | 16.1 | 30.6 | 40 min |
| 2026 | Jan-Jun only | 22 | 13.8 | 30.3 | 20 min |

\* individual totals are only available on some public checklist pages.

That raw decline is **heavily confounded by effort**. In 2026, for example, many checklists were short or incidental; an incidental incomplete list like this one is obviously not comparable to a long complete walk. [incidental 6 Apr 2026 checklist](https://ebird.org/checklist/S317826540), [complete traveling 23 Feb 2026 checklist](https://ebird.org/checklist/S303183063)

When I restricted the sample to more comparable checklists only, meaning:
- `Complete`
- `Stationary` or short `Traveling`
- at least `20 min`
- and `<= 2.5 km` for traveling lists

the pattern changed:

| Year | Comparable checklists | Mean species/checklist | Mean individuals/checklist |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2024 | 29 | 26.0 | 61.3 |
| 2025 | 68 | 19.2 | 39.3 |
| 2026 | 8 | 23.8 | 61.6 |

That is **not a monotonic trend**. It looks more like a **2025 dip plus a 2026 rebound**, but 2026 is based on only 8 comparable checklists and covers only part of the year, so I would not call that rebound definitive either.

## Is The Trend Real Enough To Guide Restoration?
Not on its own.

Three reasons:

1. **The site does not have five years of public hotspot history.**  
   The usable hotspot record starts only in late 2024. That alone prevents a real five-year trend estimate. [recent checklists](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021/recent-checklists)

2. **Observer effort changed a lot.**  
   The mix of `Stationary`, `Traveling`, and `Incidental` lists shifts by year, and median checklist duration drops from about 53 minutes in 2024 to 20 minutes in 2026 in the raw set. That can easily create a false decline in birds seen.

3. **Season coverage is uneven.**  
   2024 is mostly Oct-Dec; 2026 is Jan-Jun. In a landscape with migrants and strong wet/dry season structure, that is not apples-to-apples.

So if the decision is, “Should we change restoration strategy because birds are clearly rising/falling?”, my answer is **no, the public trend is not robust enough for that**.

## What *Is* Solid Enough To Use
What does look real enough is the site's **high bird-use potential and landscape value**.

The hotspot already shows **137 species all-time** and **80 species recorded in 2026 so far** on the public bird list. [bird list](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021/bird-list?yr=2026), [illustrated checklist](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021/illustrated-checklist?yr=2026)

That fits broader landscape evidence:
- an older Hosur Forest Division avifauna note recorded **94 species** and emphasizes the mix of dry deciduous forest, riverine habitat, and wetlands as bird-supporting habitat; it also notes that the Chinnar originates at `Thally`, in the same broader landscape. [Govindaraj 2009](https://docslib.org/doc/8961392/avifauna-of-hosur-forest-division-eastern-ghats-southern-india-kannan-govindaraj)
- a 2025 district terrestrial bird census recorded **180 species** across Krishnagiri reserve forests. [Times of India, 17 Mar 2025](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/coimbatore/180-species-recorded-in-terrestrial-bird-census-at-reserve-forests-in-krishnagiri/articleshow/119086765.cms)

That is enough to support restoration choices aimed at **habitat heterogeneity**, not enough to justify reacting to a supposed site-level decline. In practice, the public data support:
- keeping a **mosaic** of scrub, native dry deciduous woodland, edge, and wetland/lake margin
- protecting **water reliability and shallow wet edges**
- preserving **structural complexity** rather than simplifying habitat for a small target set of species

## Method
I used only public sources:
- the `EBTL` project site to identify the place [ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/)
- the public `eBird` hotspot and recent checklist pages for `Elephants by the Lake` [overview](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021), [recent checklists](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021/recent-checklists)
- direct public checklist pages to validate protocol, duration, species totals, individuals, and map coordinates, because the summary page sometimes mismatched checklist totals [example 1](https://ebird.org/checklist/S304431787), [example 2](https://ebird.org/checklist/S303183063), [example 3](https://ebird.org/checklist/S317826540)

I then summarized both:
- all validated checklist pages
- a stricter subset of comparable complete lists

If you want the next useful step, it would be a **standardized monthly bird protocol at EBTL**: same route, same start time, same duration, complete lists only. One year of that would be more decision-useful than the entire current opportunistic public record.The background checks finished successfully and confirmed the earlier conclusion.

They validated the public `eBird` checklist pages directly, filtered them to the `Elephants by the Lake` hotspot, and recomputed the yearly metrics from the checklist HTML rather than the summary page. The normalized result still shows: no defensible five-year trend, a likely effort-driven dip in 2025, and no strong evidence of a sustained increase or decline that is solid enough to steer restoration choices by itself.

No further follow-up was needed after those runs. If helpful, I can next turn this into a short decision memo with:
- `What we know`
- `What we don't know`
- `What monitoring to start now`

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) - A forest restoration project in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu

Over decades, the dry deciduous forests of our country have been stripped and exploited for commercial use. As native forests receded to only higher elevations of hills, creatures of the forests have also lost their footing in the valley. EBTL lies in one of those valleys. In the foothills of a degraded forest.

These 70 acres now 'belong' to us. How wonderful would it be if the other creatures also echoed the same thought? Our goal is to help the forest regain its rich biodiversity.

The year we began work, a few elephants came to the land, something that had never happened in the last many decades. We decided to call this project.

# Elephants By The Lake!

# The map of EBTL

Once you step into the hills around EBTL there are remnants of a once thriving forest; bird calls, fresh bear tracks, the jumping away of a troupe of langurs, trees in bloom or seed, spiders waiting for a catch, the scuffling across of a monitor lizard, a bird of prey gliding above.

Unfortunately this biodiverse ecosystem of the Eastern Ghats has been almost eradicated in terms of its area, but for a few hilly pockets where the tough terrain has made it too difficult for people to interfere.

Hopefully in time, the land will begin a cycle of regeneration where at a point, this space can become a safe corner for some of the rarer and threatened flora of the Eastern Ghats to flourish and wildlife can reinhabit the land.

# What happens at EBTL

#### Forest restoration

EBTL, primarily is focused on the native flora of the dry decidious forests of the South Deccan plateau.

#### Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies

We have established a dedicated in-house field research initiative at our campus in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, to address critical gaps in knowledge about Eastern Ghats biodiversity, ecology, and conservation priorities.

#### Organic farming

A small percentage of land we own is allotted for farming where we grow paddy, pulses, millets and vegetables.

#### Farmer's Collective

We work very closely with the nearby village of Chinnathamandrapalli. The villagers play a vital role in all the work we undertake. We have enabled a collective of women working towards value added products. They also manage our farm lands and campus.

# Farmer's Collective

We promote land stewardship and sustainable farming by employing the local community and supporting a farmers collective to create value-added products. Our goal is to provide eco-friendly job opportunities to counter urban migration among the younger generation.

content.text: The `recent checklists` page does expose individual checklist dates and species totals, so I’m parsing it now to see whether the yearly filter works and what the observation effort looks like by year.

args.command:
python - <<'PY'
import re, glob, os
files = glob.glob('/root/.cursor/projects/work/agent-tools/*.txt')
for f in files:
    if os.path.getsize(f) < 10000: 
        continue
    txt = open(f, encoding='utf-8').read()
    years = re.findall(r'###\s+\d{1,2}\s+\w+\s+(20\d{2})', txt)
    if years:
        from collections import Counter
        c=Counter(years)
        print(os.path.basename(f), sorted(c.items())[:3], '...', sorted(c.items())[-3:], 'n=', len(years))
PY

The survey recorded mammal and reptile species by (1) direct sighting, (2) indirect evidences such as the droppings, pug/hoof/pad marks and feeding signs and (3) interviews with local inhabitants using photographs to gather information on the presence of mammals and reptilian species in the region both at present and in the past. Participants were divided into three teams with each team having 4–5 people. On 1st August there were 3 teams going to the trek paths 1, 2 and 3. On 2nd August there were 2 teams that took paths 4 and 5. Background materials such as a map of the study area, documents of pug/hoof/pad marks of larger mammals, survey methods, and data sheets along with a GPS unit were given to each group. Due to the heavy rain on 31st evening many footprints could easily be seen on the wet ground on 1st August. Most commonly seen footprint was wild pig (Sus scrofa), elephants (Elephas maximus) and spotted deer (Axis axis). Teams also recorded the foot prints of Leopard (Panthera Pardus), Sloth bear (Melursus ursinus), Indian hare (Lepus nigricollis) and Indian porcupine (Hystrix indica). Mammals sighted during the survey were Bonnet Macaque (Macaca radiata), Common Indian Mongoose (Herpestes javanicus) and Three-striped palm squirrel (Funambulus palmarum). Bird sightings were also recorded in the survey, and some of the amateur bird watchers felt that Thally area was exceptional for raptors. One of the teams also recorded a species of butterfly, Red Admiral, which is known found mostly in the wetter parts of the Western Ghats. The herpertologists also recorded an unidentified species of toad, which did not belong of any of the genuses that they were familiar with. unique preserving order seen=set(); items=[] for date,cid in entries: if cid not in seen: seen.add(cid); items.append((date,cid)) print('unique ids', len(items)) headers={'User-Agent':'Mozilla/5.0'} def parse_html(date,cid): url=f'https://ebird.org/checklist/{cid}' r=requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30) html=r.text def m(pattern, flags=re.S): mm=re.search(pattern, html, flags) return mm.group(1).strip() if mm else None location=m(r'Location\s*.*?]*>(.*?)') or m(r'Location\s*.*?]*>(.*?)') protocol=m(r'Protocol:\s*\s*([^<\n]+)') or m(r'Protocol:\s*([^<\n]+)') complete=('Incomplete' not in html) if 'Complete' in html or 'Incomplete' in html else None duration=m(r'Duration:\s*\s*([^<\n]+)') or m(r'Duration:\s*([^<\n]+)') distance=m(r'Distance:\s*\s*([^<\n]+)') or m(r'Distance:\s*([^<\n]+)') owner=m(r'Owner\s*.*?]*>(.*?)') or m(r'Owner\s*(.*?)\s*]*>\s*(\d+)') if not species: species=m(r'## Totals.*?(\d+)\s*Species Observed') individuals=m(r'Species Observed.*?(\d+)\s*individuals') or m(r'## Totals.*?Species Observed\s*(\d+)\s*individuals') date_full=m(r'## Main Details.*?]*>([^<]*20\d{2}[^<]*)') or date return { 'cid':cid,'date_hint':date,'date_full':date_full,'location':location,'protocol':protocol, 'complete':complete,'duration':duration,'distance':distance,'owner':owner, 'species': int(species) if species else None, 'individuals': int(individuals) if individuals else None, 'status':r.status_code, } rows=[] with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as ex: futs={ex.submit(parse_html,date,cid):(date,cid) for date,cid in items} for i,f in enumerate(as_completed(futs),1): try: rows.append(f.result()) except Exception as e: rows.append({'cid':futs[f][1],'error':str(e)}) if i%25==0: print('done', i) print('rows', len(rows), 'errors', sum(1 for r in rows if 'error' in r)) # keep only EBTL location rows=[r for r in rows if r.get('location') and 'Elephants by the Lake' in r['location']] print('ebtl rows', len(rows)) # show sample problematic for r in rows[:3]: print(r) # aggregate by year for r in rows: m=re.search(r'(20\d{2})', r['date_full'] or r['date_hint']) r['year']=int(m.group(1)) if m else None # duration in minutes dur=r['duration'] mins=None if dur: hh=mm=0 m1=re.search(r'(\d+)\s*hr', dur) m2=re.search(r'(\d+)\s*min', dur) if m1 or m2: hh=int(m1.group(1)) if m1 else 0 mm=int(m2.group(1)) if m2 else 0 mins=hh*60+mm r['minutes']=mins dist=r['distance'] km=None if dist: m3=re.search(r'([0-9.]+)\s*km', dist) if m3: km=float(m3.group(1)) r['km']=km for y in sorted({r['year'] for r in rows if r['year']}): vals=[r for r in rows if r['year']==y] comp=[r for r in vals if r['complete'] and r['species'] is not None] strict=[r for r in comp if (r['minutes'] or 0)>=20 and ((r['protocol']=='Stationary') or (r['protocol']=='Traveling' and (r['km'] is not None and r['km']<=2.5)))] print('\nYEAR', y, 'all', len(vals), 'complete', len(comp), 'strict', len(strict), 'protocols', Counter(r['protocol'] for r in vals)) for name, subset in [('all', vals), ('complete', comp), ('strict', strict)]: s=[r['species'] for r in subset if r['species'] is not None] ind=[r['individuals'] for r in subset if r['individuals'] is not None] if s: print(name, 'species_mean', round(statistics.mean(s),1), 'species_med', statistics.median(s), 'n', len(s)) if ind: print(name, 'individuals_mean', round(statistics.mean(ind),1), 'individuals_med', statistics.median(ind), 'n_ind', len(ind)) PY

CoP16 Prop. 15 Deletion of Grey Junglefowl Gallus sonneratii from Appendix II Proponent: Switzerland, as Depositary Government, at the Request of the Animals Committee (prepared by New Zealand) Summary: The Grey Junglefowl Gallus sonneratii is endemic to India and inhabits subtropical and tropical moist forests, bamboo thickets, open woodlands and dry deciduous shrubland. The species has a wide range, estimated at around 1 million km2. It is believed to be affected by habitat loss and by some illegal hunting for its meat for domestic consumption. Good populations are likely now to be mainly confined to protected areas. The overall population is believed likely to be declining, though not at a rate fast enough to merit classifying the species as threatened. It was assessed as of Least Concern in 2012 by BirdLife International. Gallus sonneratii was one of several species of Galliform included in Appendix II in 1975 owing to concerns about the international trade in their feathers – the males possess long neck hackles (elongated feathers) with very distinctive patterning, which are in demand for making fishing flies. In the period 2000–2010, nearly 240 000 G. sonneratii feathers were recorded in the CITES trade database as in international trade; 99% of these were reported as coming from captive- bred birds and virtually all exported from non-range States. Over half were exported from the UK to the USA in 2001. Very little trade in feathers has been reported since 2004. There is a small amount of trade in live, captive-bred birds. The species is reported to be easy to keep in captivity.

### Genetic Endangerment of Wild Red Junglefowl Gallus Gallus?

Genetic Endangerment of Wild Red Junglefowl Gallus Gallus?

Bird Conservation International (1999) 9:387-394. © BirdLife International 1999 Genetic endangerment of wild Red Junglefowl Gallus gallus? A. TOWNSEND PETERSON and I. LEHR BRISBIN, JR Summary Domestic chickens were derived from the wild Red Junglefowl Gallus gallus. A survey of 745 museum specimens of Red Junglefowl suggests that most wild populations have been contaminated genetically by introgression of genes from domestic or feral chickens. A male eclipse plumage, which appears to be an indicator of pure wild genotypes, was found in populations in the western and central portions of the species's range, but not in the easternmost populations. Eclipse plumages probably disappeared from extreme south-eastern Asia and the Philippines prior to the advent of intensive scientific collecting (about i860) and have not been observed in Malaysia and neighbouring countries since the 1920s. Populations exhibiting eclipse plumages were found in north-eastern India as late as the 1960s, but the dense human populations there make their continu- ing genetic integrity uncertain. These data suggest that surveys of wild and cap- tive populations should be undertaken to assess the genetic integrity of this spe- cies. A re-evaluation of the conservation status of Red Junglefowl might then follow. Introduction The evolution of chickens can be conceived of as a three-step process: (1) evolu- tion and speciation of wild ancestors, (2) domestication, and (3) diversification into numerous varieties under artificial selection by humans (Stevens 1991). We suggest an additional process: subsequent replacement of wild genes through hybridization with feral or free-ranging domestic stock. This process may have caused, or may now be causing, the genetic extinction of wild populations.

Krishnagiri: A total of 180 bird species were identified and recorded during the synchronised terrestrial bird census held on March 15 and 16 in reserve forests across Krishnagiri district.
Bakan Jagdish Sudhakar, wildlife warden, Hosur forest division said, "A total of 100 people participated in the census, including 30 forest staff, 70 volunteers, and ornithologists." He added that the team began their work at 6am and continued until 11pm, visiting approximately 25 locations during the day and five at night.
Notable species recorded included the Bay-backed Shrike, Changeable Hawk Eagle, Common Iora, Coppersmith Barbet, Jordan's Nightjar, Indian Robin, Jerdon's Bushlark, Laughing Dove, Pied Bush Chat, Purple Rumped Sunbird, Shikra, and Spotted Owlet.
Earlier on March 8 and 9, a wetland bird census was held in the district during which 200 bird species were recorded. The officer added that the census report will be sent to the Tamil Nadu government.

## Bottom Line
No credible five-year increase or decline can be established yet for birds at `Elephants by the Lake`.

The public record at the actual `eBird` hotspot for `Elephants by the Lake` only runs from **10 Oct 2024 to 22 Jun 2026**, not five full years, and the checklist mix changes a lot across time. The raw public data show an apparent dip in 2025, but that signal is **not stable enough** to treat as a real biological decline or increase for restoration planning. The safest reading is: **bird use of the site looks variable, not clearly trending up or down**. [eBird hotspot](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021), [recent checklists](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021/recent-checklists), [sample checklist with map link](https://ebird.org/checklist/S304431787)

## What The Public Data Say
I anchored the analysis to the `eBird` hotspot associated with the restoration site in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu. `EBTL` itself describes the project as a 70-acre restoration site in the foothills of degraded Eastern Ghats forest near Krishnagiri. [EBTL site](https://ebtl.earth/)

From the public hotspot record, I extracted **168 checklist links** and successfully validated **161 public checklist pages** at the same hotspot name and coordinate (`12.7338913,78.1833887`) from the map links on the checklist pages. [recent checklists](https://ebird.org/region/L36453021/recent-checklists), [28 Feb 2026 checklist](https://ebird.org/checklist/S304431787), [23 Feb 2026 checklist](https://ebird.org/checklist/S303183063)

Using those validated checklists, the raw yearly pattern looks like this:

| Year | Date coverage | Checklists used | Mean species/checklist | Mean individuals/checklist* | Median duration |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2024 | Oct-Dec only | 34 | 23.3 | 53.2 | 53 min |
| 2025 | full year | 105 | 16.1 | 30.6 | 40 min |
| 2026 | Jan-Jun only | 22 | 13.8 | 30.3 | 20 min |

\* individual totals are only available on some public checklist pages.

That raw decline is **heavily confounded by effort**. In 2026, for example, many checklists were short or incidental; an incidental incomplete list like this one is obviously not comparable to a long complete walk. [incidental 6 Apr 2026 checklist](https://ebird.org/checklist/S317826540), [complete traveling 23 Feb 2026 checklist](https://ebird.org/checklist/S303183063)

When I restricted the sample to more comparable checklists only, meaning:
- `Complete`
- `Stationary` or short `Traveling`
- at least `20 min`
- and `<= 2.5 km` for traveling lists

the pattern changed:

| Year | Comparable checklists | Mean species/checklist | Mean individuals/checklist |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2024 | 29 | 26.0 | 61.3 |
| 2025 | 68 | 19.2 | 39.3 |
| 2026 | 8 | 23.8 | 61.6 |
